speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all members should welcome the opportunity provided by this notice of

July 30, 1982
Charitable Donations
motion to debate this question. We are all agreed on the importance and the value of the contribution which voluntary charitable organizations make to our society.
The issue before the House today is in what way and to what extent should governments be assisting this effort through provisions of the Income Tax Act. The extent of such governmental assistance through the tax system is already substantial. The figures for 1979 show that more than $500 million in tax revenues were forgone in the form of tax allowances by the federal government and, of course, by the nine provinces, the personal tax levies of which are linked to the federal tax law under tax collection agreements.
We are, of course, familiar with the fact that Quebec, which levies its own income tax, also grants a similar deduction for charitable donations. This represents a substantial proportion, perhaps as much as one third of total contributions by individuals and businesses to these charities.
I should like to explain that the present income tax system has two provisions relating to charitable donations. First, an individual who has donated more than $100 in charitable givings may deduct the total of those donations from income in computing income tax. The claim must be accompanied of course by individual receipts. The deduction cannot exceed 20 per cent of net income for the year, although any excess may be carried forward and deducted in the following year. This 20 per cent ceiling is a limiting factor for a very few taxpayers only.
Second, the tax system allows a flat $100 deduction from income for taxpayers whose combined charitable donations and claimable medical expenses do not exceed $100. For all practical purposes, this standard $100 deduction is relevant to charitable donation alone. This is because taxpayers may claim deductions for medical expenses only when these expenses exceed 3 per cent of net income, and only a relatively small percentage of taxpayers qualify for such medical expense deductions. This is an important factor when we come to consider one of the proposals in the motion relating to the $100 standard deduction.
I suggest there are three principal considerations to be borne in mind in discussing what whould best be done on this issue.
First, the government should provide some incentive for charitable giving, and not just any incentive, regardless of cost. There is not much point in granting a $10 tax incentive in order to generate a $5 charitable gift.
Second, the incentive should prefereably be an equitable one. This means that donors at different income levels should receive equal incentive benefits for donations of equal size.
Let me note that these first two considerations are the base and have been put forward as the basic objectives outlined by the national voluntary organizations in their submission to the Canadian government.
Third, in this period of fiscal restraint, hon. members must be very concerned at what will be the impact on our budgetary deficit of any new tax provision.
It is on that last point that we run into the most serious problem with the proposal before us. It is estimated by the Department of Finance that to implement these suggested changes would cost more than $500 million in forgone revenues in addition to the current tax incentive costs. In effect, we are being asked to double the level of fiscal support for charitable giving.
Such an increase of half a billion dollars in the over-all deficit position of governments cannot be justified under the present circumstances, if fiscal restraint is to have any meaning at all. Admittedly it can be argued that the proposed changes could provide some additional incentive for charitable giving, and ensure some more equity in our tax arrangements. These are worthwhile objectives, but I suggest we wdl have to look at the price tag.
We have on this side of the House been deeply concerned, as everyone else has, by the grave growth of problems in the economic situations throughout the world. We have seen that this has brought about a kind of fiscal problem because when you have a recession in the world, when you have a recessionary economy, then naturally your businesses will not flourish, they will not make as much profit, individuals will not be as well employed, they will not be making as large a salary, and therefore the income that is derived is smaller, and the revenues for the government therefore will become smaller.
One of the major byproducts of this, as we have seen, is that in the new budget a large part of the increase in our deficit has come from the need to provide increased unemployment insurance and also which is very important, we find there is a reduction in the size of the income that is derived. We are receiving a smaller income into the federal treasuries, less revenue. Some of us perhaps are aware of the fact that there are two ways to make money, one is to earn it and the other is to save it. When less money is coming in it is just as bad as if you were spending more money. That is the practical problem.
This proposal before us now means an addition to the half billion dollars that the government is already forgiving or providing as a tax incentive to the people of Canada. In other words, the Canadian tax system provides relief of approximately one half billion dollars now to the taxpayers who can use these funds as they contribute to charitable causes and charitable donations. This one half billion dollars less, is something which already is being used as an incentive by the federal government to bring private contributions to charitable organizations. That is a contribution, which means one-half billion dollars less money to the treasury.
Now, the new proposal which we have in this resolution is something with which I greatly sympathize. But what I have to point out, in order to recognize responsibly what it means, is that the figures that have been estimated by the finance department to be the costs would add another one-half billion dollars of tax forgiveness. That means that one-half billion dollars less would be going into the federal treasury. That would mean, in effect, a total subsidy of $1 billion.
July 30, 1982

1 do not feel too concerned about this fact for a number of reasons which I would like to explain. I must say, however, that I do find there is some sad inconsistency when members of the opposition rise daily during question period to call for additional spending by the government on programs to relieve the hardship suffered by Canadians because of the economic problems which exist today in Canada and the world. As those members rise to speak daily, they call for greater government relief, which means spending more money but, on the other hand, these same members or their colleagues rise on another day to criticize the government for the fact that it has projected a high fiscal deficit for the year. Indeed, one can see that if they were to be consistent they would do either one or the other. You can hardly call for more spending which increases the deficit and at the same time criticize the government for the large deficit which exists.
This particular resolution is an example of the kind of worthwhile project that might be suggested but which would cost money. If it were a project that were suggested during affluent times, when there was a growing gross national product, it would be easier to understand that it could be implemented. However, at a time when we are calling for restraint, this suggestion creates some difficulty for us.
This means that we have to ask ourselves why the official opposition cannot get its act together. I would call upon those members to find a more integrated or rationalized policy through which they could provide a consistent approach. If I were to look at it in a less than kind manner, I might suggest that it might be good politics for the official opposition to plead for more spending to help those who are hurting while calling for restraint to please those who know that we cannot just throw money away to solve our problems at this time. In that way, maybe it is thought they can get the best of both worlds.
In some ways perhaps the NDP can be considered to be more consistent since they call incessantly for increasing spending without calling for the same restraints at the same time.
We on this side of the House know that the buck stops with us. It is a tragedy that we cannot spend more on programs to reduce the suffering of Canadians because we have to exercise restraint. We see a similar policy being carried out in many other countries at the present time. We see this policy in western European countries and in the United States.
No one could be more aware than I of the importance of charitable donations. No one could be more sensitive or feel more sympathetic than I to the objectives expressed in this resolution. I support the ideas proposed in this motion, but nevertheless I must assume the responsibility of pointing out that it will cost a price. I must also point out that at this particular juncture in our economic recovery in Canada, it is not exactly a most welcome time for such a change.
Why do I feel sympathetic to the proposals in this motion? I feel that if responsible voluntary groups receive more money
Charitable Donations
they can make better use of the money than if the government had to spend it. If all things are equal, if a program must be carried out, I feel that it can be carried out with greater personal devotion, commitment and dedication by a responsible charitable or voluntary organization than it can be by a federal, provincial, or any government. Therefore, I am quite persuaded that if a program must be carried out, I would much rather contribute the money, in terms of using less money to be spent with greater effectiveness, to the organization in question than contribute to the treasuries of an impersonal government.
I believe that dedicated workers can achieve more than bureaucrats, not because bureaucrats are heartless people but because the very system tends to defeat the ability to create that sense of commitment and devotion through its largeness and impersonality. The same is not true of a voluntary organization.
Having worked as the national director of the League of Human Rights of B'nai Brith, which is a charitable organization, I had an opportunity to experience this at first hand. With respect to some of the programs which we conducted with voluntary help, I know that it costs the province 26 times in paid employee time to conduct the same kind of institutional or educational conference. We could do it for less because we had dedicated volunteers who contributed endless amounts of time, overtime and effort to the cause as well as facilities which were already available in terms of overhead. In other words, there were contributions in kind, contributions in terms of employee commitment and volunteer commitment. Without that volunteer commitment the province had to pay 26 times more for the program than it cost the organization.
Not only have I seen this as someone who has administered a national charitable institution, I see the same things in my riding. I have seen that non-profit charitable organizations can do far more with the same amount of money.
For this reason I think governments tend quite correctly, to give grants to such organizations because they know it will be handled more efficiently and provide greater flexibility when carried out by non-profit charitable organizations. For example, there is the Italian-Canadian Benevolent Corporation which was able, through its personal attention to human feelings, to create an amazing and unique type of senior citizens' program in a setting which would be familiar to the origins of those people. They provided an atmosphere for people in their old age which enabled them to feel that they were in an environment which had flowers and fountains similar to what they had in their country of origin. In that sense, one can find that in the voluntary work of an organization which understands the people for whom it is working, which understands the needs of those people when it was constructing the residence known as Villa Columbo. The same situation is true so far as the new apartments it is constructing are concerned. The same thing could be said for St. Hilda's Towers. A second tower is now being completed for older adults. It has been created to provide a community feeling for

July 30, 1982
Charitable Donations
those people, a feeling which they could not experience in an impersonal, if you will, bureaucratic or government institution.
The applicaton of voluntary assistance, work and dedication of this type demonstrates part of Canada's way of life. I simply want to say that from my own personal experience and from what I see in my riding, when I look at the Baycrest Centre for geriatric care and a number of other places which are run by volunteers, I believe that the money given to them is more sympathetically and carefully spent than if it were given to a bureaucracy. On the one hand, if money has to be spent it is better to provide that incentive and to contribute to voluntary institutions and the voluntary sector. Consequently, the Income Tax Act should be amended to provide that incentive. On the other hand, we have to take into account what it would mean to take $500 million more out of the federal treasury if we are not going to spend it anyway. I suggest they will not spend it in any way right now.
In conclusion if I were able to be encouraging about what we should do here, in the future, I would say that a committee of Members of Parliament should consider, study and discuss how the Income Tax Act can be adjusted so that it will be more equitable in the field of charitable contributions, a committee which would make realistic suggestions in terms of our restraint program, yet provide encouragement to that sector of our society which can do the job more effectively than the federal government or, for that matter, the provincial and municipal governments.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARITABLE GIFTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I encourage the hon. member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille) to follow up on his last proposal. He may wish to refer to the records of the House and to the proposal put forward by the Clark government to establish a task force on voluntarism. He may wish to encourage the government that he supports to move in the direction of that proposal. It is indeed timely of the government to agree to enter into today's debate on how it might come to support the role of the voluntary sector in Canadian society.
In entering this debate, I want to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche), on making such a well-marshalled defence of the motion he originally tabled here in the House on June 9, 1980, so that hon. members have felt that today's continuation of the debate is not only warranted but that it is a motion which they can genuinely and generally, in a non-partisan way, advocate on all sides of the House. I look forward, as do Canada's over three million volunteers, to a signal from the government that it has used these intervening two years to develop a comprehensive framework for the early implementation of tax changes embodied in the motion. 1 hope that the government is not totally preoccupied with the familiar arguments we have heard echoed from the Department of Finance.
It is important to recall the intent with which this motion was originally introduced. The hon. member for Edmonton South said:

The purpose of the motion that I am bringing before the House today is to help voluntary organizations make a greater contribution to the quality of life in Canada. Specifically, I am urging the government to amend the Income Tax Act; first, to remove the standard $100 deduction for charitable donations and, second, to replace the standard deduction with a 50 per cent tax credit along with the option of continuing to deduct charitable contributions from taxable income if it is in the taxpayer's interest to do so.

We note that spokespersons from the government side have often spoken of their appreciation of the irreplaceable contribution made by Canada's voluntary sector. What they have never done, however, is to indicate the concrete ways in which the government they support can provide much needed incentives to Canadian taxpayers for the increase in charitable contributions.
The tax reforms spelled out in this motion were first advocated by the national voluntary organizations, a coalition representing over 120 large and small Canadian agencies. Known widely as the give-and-take proposal, and the type of bulletin I have in my hand has gone into all members' offices, these reforms are the product of years of expert research and extensive consultation with Canadian volunteers, as well as negotiations with officials from the Department of Finance, National Revenue, and the Secretary of State.
The most recent results of this ongoing research-negotiation process indicate confirmation of the original national voluntary organizations' position, that is, if the give and take proposal had been implemented in 1980, as the hon. member for Edmonton South suggested, federal and provincial governments would have saved money. Yes, Mr. Speaker, the recently published results of Statistics Canada's 1980 audit of returns provided to Revenue Canada by all registered charities provide government-funded evidence. It is time the government incorporated this evidence into its policy and its thinking rather than continuing to parrot the type of comment we have just heard.
Indeed the chief statistician of Statistics Canada, Dr. Martin B. Wilk, has indicated this in writing to the N.V.O. in a memorandum of June 16, this year:
Since, in 1980, the total cost of the charitable deduction system was $762 million, it appears that the contention the N.V.O. have been making for three years, (that the government could switch to a 50 per cent tax credit at no additional cost), is correct.
Government supporters are quite right in pointing out that as these reforms are implemented, the cost to the government in forgone revenues will increase. Experience with the implementation of the tax changes affecting donations to political parties has shown that it takes up to six years for a behavioural change in the patterns of taxpayer contributions to become evident. Current estimates indicate that it will take up to five years, after implementation, for the cost of give and take reforms to be known. At that point the cost to government
July 30, 1982

in forgone revenues, which concerned the hon. member, will be $ 1 for every $2 going directly to charity.
The last time this motion was before the House, over two years ago, government spokespersons complained about the cost of implementing this motion. Indeed, the then parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) said:
-at a time when we are worrying about reducing our present federal deficit, we should not be thinking about adding another half billion dollars to the combined federal-provincial deficits.
The same member made a similar complaint during the November 24, 1980, debate of my private member's motion to:
-provide volunteer agencies with financial aid to support their communications and fund-raising activities, so that a greater portion of available funds could be freed for their intended charitable uses.
And again, in the June 5, 1981, debate on my private member's Bill C-233, an act to encourage the role of the voluntary sector in Canadian society, another government spokesperson complained that:
-we must not always depend upon the government. Charities already have available to them various mechanisms to obtain assistance.
As you see, the government has long maintained that acceptance and implementation of the reforms as put forward in the motion before us again today are too expensive because of an apparent worsening of the federal deficit position.
I believe that the new information available from the Statistics Canada research, from the work of the national voluntary organizations and from the important investigations carried on in our universities, such as the contribution made by Professor Douglas McCready in the Department of Business and Economics at Wilfrid Laurier University, clearly demonstrate a new direction which the government would be well advised to follow.
Let us for a moment consider the ultimate costs to governments in forgone revenues resulting from the implementation of the give and take proposal, about which we have just heard a litany, and the cost to the federal treasury relating to large scale, multi-million dollar job creation schemes, familiar under this government.
Let me ask the government and its supporters to think of the voluntary sector as an engine for employment creation. Let us begin to think of this motion's tax reforms as a mechanism for government investment in creating jobs during record unemployment, instead of thinking in terms of increased government spending, which hon. members opposite are quite right in saying we can ill afford given the current disastrous deficit levels.
Unfortunately, this government has never measured the employment capacity of the voluntary sector. We have been waiting since January 1981 for a strategy on the voluntary sector. It was promised by the previous secretary of state, reiterated by the present Secretary of State (Mr. Regan), but is yet to see the light of day.
Charitable Donations
To my surprise this government has never developed a mechanism to begin measuring the number or type of employment opportunities created by the voluntary sector. This is so despite the fact that there are 47,000 charitable agencies, units, if you will, presently active in this country. I invite hon. members to compare this total with the fact that there are only 31,000 manufacturing units operating in Canada. The government has never bothered to measure the contribution made by the voluntary sector to Canada's gross national product. While it is difficult to be sure of the number of jobs provided by charitable agencies, it is quite clear that this is an extremely labour-intensive sector. High technology is too expensive. These are people at work, often in their two's, four's and six's. Not only that, the vast majority of those employed by charitable agencies are women, youth, handicapped persons, low-income and laid-off workers, the very segments of our population currently experiencing such tragic unemployment levels and alienation.
Let me make another reflection on why this government ought to reconsider its definition. Think for a moment of the voluntary sector and its ability to train and retrain. This has always been an essential feature of the voluntary sector as it seeks to meet the changing social needs of our society. Women learn skills which help them to bridge the re-entry phase in joining or returning to the work force. Our youth receive initial training and skills which they ultimately put to use in the challenging employment of serving their fellow Canadians. There is no parallel for the training of young people that is inherent in the voluntary sector.
In terms of cost effectiveness, this training and retraining aspect surely deserves the attention of a minister of finance anxious to deal with the deficit and a minister of employment and immigration anxious to somehow equip and motivate Canadians. For example, the professionals who now support the irreplaceable services across this country of the YMCA were in their youth in large part initially trained by the same voluntary agency.
What I am asking the government to do in support of the very positive and manageable motion brought forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton South, is to consider the charitable tax credit before us as an employment creation tool in terms of its present strategy. Here is a sector which has enormous potential to employ those target groups about whose current unemployment we are all so concerned. At the same time as these people find gainful employment, they will be filling the gap left behind by the government's withdrawal and threatened cutback of many of the social services which can no longer be financially supported. I encourage the government, and I invite the parliamentary secretary in any response that he may make, to reflect upon the changes of the last two years since this bill was introduced. I urge him to rethink the relationship between the Canadian taxpayer and his society, between the old-style big government social spending schemes and the proven record of our voluntary sector. I urge the government to set free through the early acceptance of this mechanism the nation's voluntary and charitable agencies in

July 30, 1982
Charitable Donations
order that in a time of deep national crisis, the morale, sense of purpose and sense of belonging which is unique to those three million Canadian volunteers may be fully employed from the Atlantic to the Pacific in this land.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARITABLE GIFTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going to be brief. I want to talk about some of the implications for the tax system in this proposal. My colleague from Shef-ford, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State (Mr. Lapierre), has some comments to make about the give-and-take idea and the proposals of the national voluntary organizations. Therefore, I will be quick.
First, this is a worthy idea to study. It is certainly deserving of our continued support to see if it will indeed fly as a good idea. We have to make a balance between the needs of a voluntary society and the need to avoid dependence on the tax system. 1 think the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) will agree with that.
I would like to suggest some of the complexities in this whole area that he has not raised. These are quite apart from the matters of voluntary activity or the question of merits of the individual groups which would benefit from an expanded tax credit.
Last November during the tax changes introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), a debate arose about the use of the tax system to create incentives similar to this one. Should we use deductions in the tax system to create incentives or should we use the tax system simply to finance government? That is a very important point.
When the minister introduced his changes last November, he did two things. He removed some of the prior incentives in the tax system. He also reduced the marginal tax rate. He returned the savings to the taxpayer. In many cases those were very substantial savings.
When we develop tax incentives, as we found both last November and in our experiences following last November, we also develop an encouragement for people to use those incentives for purposes beyond which they were originally debated and designed. We create incentives for all kinds of activities in one area at the exclusion of other areas. We develop a very complicated set of encouragements in the tax system to channel money to avoid taxes, to shelter money from taxes rather than to simply encourage the worthwile behaviour, in this case the voluntary activity.
Some of the changes introduced last November affected business activity or personal activity. They were all considered by various taxpayers to be worthy deductions. In each case there were people ready to defend those deductions. However, the fundamental point is that those deductions had created incentives for taxpayers to shelter income from the tax man. Sometimes those shelters were not the ones that had originally been designed or intended.
The government has asked people to remember some very simple principles about tax incentives. Tax incentives are tax expenditures. Take as an example ten people living on a desert island. If in this heavenly example it costs $100 to operate the desert island, each of those ten people would pay $10 toward
the operation of that island. If one person came along with a desired goal and talked the others into giving him an exemption, then everyone else would have to pick up that person's share of the burden. Where everyone had previously been paying $10 each, they would now have to pay $11 and change to operate the island. If we add a few zeroes to my example the point is the same for the finances of the Government of Canada. If we start to give people more and more exemptions from their tax, then the rest of the country has to pick up the slack. In many cases people are able to take advantage of shelters in a way the rest of us would not approve of; they are able to find a channel into a tax shelter that the rest of us would not accept, yet we are paying for that extra burden.
It is not enough to say that we should give exemptions because these are worthy volunteer organizations. We have to come back to a more basic point and ask whether it is possible for taxpayers to use these exemptions in a way that genuine volunteers would not accept or whether it is better to avoid the problem altogether and put out the money in the form of a grant, instead of using the tax system which looks so easy but in fact is practical and easy for a lot of people, not just for the intended beneficiary.
Perhaps it would be better to give a grant the way we do under the New Horizons program, where a group of people put their minds to a project and design something that fits our goals and then gets a grant for it. We could then justify to our friends across the way and to the general public that expenditure of their money. We could say that one group came within the acceptable limits, that another group was subject to audit and that yet another group did not misspend the money. We could give that kind of assurance to Canadian taxpayers.
It is easy to say that tax incentives should be used and that volunteer groups should get some recognition from the government. I think I would agree generally with hon. members on that, but I question the method of using tax incentives.
In the desert island example, if ten people pay $100 and suddenly there are just nine people who have to find the $100, then they have to pay $11 instead of $10 and we have to justify to the nine why the tenth should be exempt. We have to make sure that we do not set up a special route where people can slip money in and hide it from the tax man.
I started out by saying that there are really two questions to answer, Mr. Speaker: how do we encourage voluntarism and how do we avoid dependence on the tax system. I hope the hon. member for Waterloo will turn his mind to the question of tax incentive versus grants. I think that question has to be answered. It is a pretty fundamental issue of public accountability, and taxpayers can go down our list of expenditures and see what we have put their money into. Hon. members, like the hon. member for Waterloo, can ask about the wisdom of each expenditure. He could not do that if we had tax incentives buried in the tax system, but he could do so with a grant
July 30, 1982

system. I wonder if the grant system is not better because of that openness.
There are some other limits to the suggestion which I think the hon. member has not discussed with us, and I hope he will give us better answers than he has so far.
In 1979, $500 million was forgone in tax revenues under the $100 standard deduction or, alternatively, under the receipted reductions. That is a lot of money, Mr. Speaker. It is a very respectable amount of support for voluntarism across the country. According to my information it represents about $ 1 in every $3 that Canadian people give to charitable organizations. If we start with these facts we realize the enormous support the government is giving as an incentive toward charitable donations. If we were to follow the scheme proposed in the motion, we would spend another $500 million annually, according to the information I was given. That $500 million would be offset, to a degree, by the kinds of considerations that the hon. member has recommended. I think we have to address ourselves to that during the period of financial restraint.
If we follow the tax incentive idea rather than a system of grants, we should also look at the problem of tax deductions or tax credits. It seems to me that a tax deduction tends to assist higher income people while a tax credit will encourage both lower and higher income people to make a contribution. It may be more equitable and more of an encouragement.
We also have to look at how we handle the medical aspects of the current flat $100 medical and charitable deduction. If we just made that a $100 medical deduction it could cost us up to $250 million annually. I do not know if we want to encourage that during a time of restraint.
Those are specific concerns that the Department of Finance has about the proposal, Mr. Speaker. We do not offer them to be a wet blanket or to ruin the proposal, but they have not been answered. There is still the problem of using a grant or tax incentive and how either is to be paid for.
I think the hon. member, who keeps thinking about these issues and presenting new ideas in a positive and inventive fashion, should be congratulated. I hope he will give us some answers to these technical questions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by strongly endorsing the proposition that Canada needs a national policy on voluntarism. Part of that consideration should be a review of the income tax provisions relating to contributions to charities and volunteer organizations in Canada. I congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche) who brought this resolution before us for debate. It deals specifically with the income tax provision that is now in force and recommends what so many volunteer organizations have endorsed as a new provision known as the give-and-take provision.
I want to deal specifically with the proposition outlined in the motion presented by the hon. member for Edmonton South and discussed by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean). First of all I should like to deal with the current provision and indicate how unfair it has become.
I am sure that hon. members are aware that the Income Tax Act provides a tax benefit in relation to charitable donations.
Charitable Donations
Approximately 88 per cent of Canadian taxpayers took advantage of that $100 deduction for charitable donations and medical expenses, whether or not they contributed any of it to charity, according to the last statistics available to me. This fact has become known over the years. It has been the subject of research and scientific inquiry, and we know that in fact 88 per cent of taxpayers who claim the $100 deduction do not donate that money or any substantial part of it to volunteer organizations. Statistics indicate that only about 20 per cent of those dollars are donated.
So we have established the fact that this deduction is not working to the benefit of voluntary organizations and charities in Canada. In addition, we have had this figure of $100 in force for almost two decades. We know, with the inflation rate we have experienced, that a proper amount by today's standards would be probably in excess of $500. So when members of the government party stand in this House and say this is a worthwhile proposition they are being less than candid because they know the deduction is not being used to benefit charities; secondly, the amount permitted is tremendously out of line given the inflation we have experienced over the last number of years. The government has to come to grips with this problem because what is at stake is the tremendous effort made by voluntary organizations across Canada, and I want to deal very briefly with that in the time remaining to me.
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that my information comes from the Committee of National Voluntary Organizations which represents approximately 130 voluntary organizations across Canada. That committee pointed out in a report to a special committee of the PC Party on the budget and the economy that the total number of Canadians to participate in voluntary work approached three million, and that is a very substantial number. That group contributed approximately 373 million working hours, the equivalent of 218,000 person-years of voluntary labour. That represents $3.5 billion in wages forgone.
So when we talk about the volunteer movement in Canada, we are talking about a very substantial economic force and one to which the government ought to give full credit. It would give that credit, Mr. Speaker, by supporting the volunteer movement and recognizing the difficulties present in legislation and by moving to make those changes in the manner proposed by my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton South, and endorsed by organizations such as the Canadian Council on Social Development and the committee of National Voluntary Organizations.
Let me deal very briefly, Mr. Speaker, with the give-and-take proposals which were endorsed in a 1977 report by the Canadian Council on Social Development entitled "Toward a National Policy on Voluntarism". First of all, the whole purpose of the give-and-take proposition is that we remove the $100 deduction and replace it with a tax credit whereby a

July 30, 1982
Charitable Donations
contributor will receive 50 cents for every dollar contributed, up to a limit of probably 20 per cent of his taxable income. Of course, if the contributor wants to take advantage of the existing provision to contribute 20 per cent of his net income to charity, he can do that but it would only apply to persons with incomes in excess of $50,000. We know that most Canadians do not have an income in that range, so what we have to do is to get ordinary Canadians contributing to these organizations. We are not going to do that with the current provision because in fact it is regressive, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and his officials know it. Not only does it not encourage contributions, it in fact discourages contributions.
We know from the debate so far, Mr. Speaker, that there are probably 50,000 volunteer organizations and charities registered under the Income Tax Act. As I said, they represent millions of Canadians. But here we are as the legislators for all Canadians actively discouraging contributions to these organizations. That is a shame not only on Parliament but particularly on the government.
I want to take the opportunity to place on the record the remarks of the chairman of the Committee of National Voluntary Organizations who pointed out the political difficulty these organizations face because they are non-partisan in nature and they suffer as a result. Their point is not always brought forward, which is simply a request for fair treatment and the development of a national policy on voluntarism to correct this unfair treatment. We have heard in the debate so far references to restraint and the need to curb government spending, but the fact of the matter is the contribution made by these organizations is a very positive one and it must be encouraged in a period of restraint. I am thinking particularly of organizations like post-secondary schools, universities and hospitals across Canada which will be faced with cutbacks in government funding. Universities, for example, receive almost 85 per cent of their funding from governments, and the other 15 per cent has to come from student fees and the private sector. We all know that students cannot afford substantial increases, in fact any increases, in tuition fees. Where will the
additional funds come from? They have to come from individuals willing to support universities in this time of need. That applies not only to universities but to hospitals and a number of other institutions which receive their funding from government and are now facing cutbacks. So when we talk about voluntary organizations, we are not only talking about organizations like the Royal Canadian Legion, 500,000 strong, which has contributed so much to volunteer services, or the voluntary firemen; we are now talking about institutions like universities and hospitals.
It may be, Mr. Speaker, that the parliamentary secretary wants to make a contribution, but my experience has been that I never received any benefit from the Liberal Party in this House in the matter of speaking in debate, and I think the previous speaker on that side overshot his time. So I will tell the parliamentary secretary something about the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) and voluntarism in this country. I have here a picture of the Secretary of State, and you know what he is doing? He is presenting a cheque for $7,800 to the Nova Scotia Volunteer Week Committee.
